entries.claim: An information disclosure is confirmed by comparing the same request sent unauthenticated and with a valid session and by differencing responses across object identifiers: if a field the unauthenticated caller should not influence differs, the response content is the disclosure.
steps: Restate the claim as an assertion about observable behaviour.
Identify the ONE request that would be true if the claim holds and false if it does not.
Run it with a control that differs in exactly one variable.
If you cannot name the control, you cannot prove the claim — park it as unverified rather than reporting it.
variation: - **Do two layers disagree about the same bytes?** — container: **do** nest the value one layer deeper (archive, template, include); **observe** a second interpretation after the first check.
- **What sits between client and sink?** — http2: **do** negotiate h2/h2c; **observe** frame-level parsing differences.
- **WHERE does the value arrive?** — header: **do** send it as a header; **observe** hop-by-hop stripping and header folding.
- **AS whom are you testing?** — anonymous: **do** send with no credentials; **observe** whether the route is reachable pre-auth.
- **What PROVES it, beyond a status code?** — differential: **do** compare against a control that differs in one variable; **observe** the difference the control did not produce.
escalation: No effect raw? Walk the encoding ladder: raw -> percent-encoded -> double-encoded -> look-alike separators, one rung at a time, never all at once.
Flat in the header? Move the SAME value to a different location (query / path / body / header / cookie). A filter on one location says nothing about the others.
Still flat? You have proven the sink is not reachable on this path, which is a RESULT. Record it and move to the next candidate rather than escalating payloads blindly.

entries.claim: Any application on an EC2 instance can read instance metadata including IAM role credentials from the link-local address 169.254.169.254, and EKS pods by default can reach the worker node's metadata the same way.
steps: Build the ladder BEFORE probing: raw, single-encoded, double-encoded, and over-long variants of the same logical value.
Send each rung with the baseline procedure (one variable changed).
Record which rung first produces an effect. That rung identifies the decoding layer the application applies, and where the check and the decode disagree.
Verify WHERE normalisation happened: reflect the value in a way only the server could compute. Client-side canonicalisation proves nothing about the server.

steps: Prove the sink reads a file at all BEFORE testing traversal: fetch a file you KNOW exists on the target and confirm real content comes back.
If you cannot get a known-good read, there is no traversal finding to report — the sink is not proven.
Then apply the traversal value and confirm the returned content is from OUTSIDE the intended directory. Content, not status code.
Reject any result where only the status line differs: proxies, error handlers and WAFs produce status differentials with no file ever read.
Establish that your out-of-band channel works AT ALL with a known true positive before drawing any conclusion from its absence.
Then test the vulnerable condition. Absence of a callback is only meaningful once the channel is proven.
Record the callback evidence (resolved host, token, timestamp) — a blind result with no artefact is not reportable.

entries.claim: A bare Unix epoch timestamp in an otherwise generic response is an information disclosure only when it can be aggregated across responses to expose an exploitable pattern, making aggregation the deciding test rather than presence.
steps: Identify the check and the use as TWO separate operations, and measure the gap between them.
Fire many parallel attempts (tens to hundreds) so at least one lands inside the window.
Vary ONLY the timing; the payload and session stay fixed.
Report a rate, not a single success: N successes in M attempts both proves the window and tells the reader whether it is practical to exploit.

steps: Capture the pre-state with a read-only request and record it.
Perform the single state change.
Read the state again THROUGH THE SAME ACCOUNT and, if a second test identity exists, through that identity too.
A change visible only to the actor proves write access, not a vulnerability. Cross-account visibility is what makes it one.
